Bilateral barbell work reduced further in Phase 3; unilateral and machine-based work becomes more prominent
Balance support (TRX or rack) offered as standard (not optional) for reverse lunges in Phase 3
Do not increase load and volume simultaneously during Phase 1 progression
At least one full rest day between each training session
Avoid training on consecutive days

# 12-Week Prenatal Strength Programme
### Client Profile & Programming Philosophy

---

## Client Overview

**Client:** Female, 30 years old | **Experience:** Advanced lifter | **Gestation at start:** 20 weeks | **Gestation at end:** ~32 weeks | **Medical clearance:** OB-approved for moderate strength training

**Key constraints driving every programming decision:**
- No supine (flat on back) positions from Week 16 onward — already in effect at programme start
- No maximal or near-maximal attempts (keep RPE ≤ 7–8; no true 1RM, 2RM, or grinding singles)
- No contact sports or high-collision activities
- Intra-abdominal pressure management becomes increasingly important as pregnancy progresses
- Centre of gravity shifts weekly — balance and proprioception must be monitored continuously
- Diastasis recti risk rises through the second and third trimester; avoid loaded spinal flexion and heavy Valsalva

**Programming goals:**
1. Maintain as much functional strength as possible through the second and early third trimester
2. Preserve posterior chain, glute, and upper-back integrity for postpartum recovery
3. Support pelvic floor health throughout
4. Keep training enjoyable, safe, and confidence-building

---

## Programme Architecture

| Phase | Weeks | Theme | Sessions/Week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 | 1–4 | Adaptation & Audit | 3 |
| Phase 2 | 5–8 | Strength Maintenance | 3 |
| Phase 3 | 9–12 | Functional Strength & Longevity | 3 |

**Session structure every week:** Two full-body strength sessions + one lower-intensity movement/accessory session. Total training time per session: 50–65 minutes. Rest periods: 90–120 seconds between working sets; longer if heart rate or perceived exertion warrants it.

**Load guidelines across all phases:**
- Working loads stay between 65–80% of estimated current 1RM (not tested — use RPE and recent training history)
- RPE cap: **7 out of 10** in Phases 1–2, dropping to **6–7** in Phase 3 as fatigue and belly size increase
- All sets should finish with at least 2–3 reps clearly "in the tank"
- Breathing: encourage exhale on exertion, avoid prolonged breath-holding; no heavy Valsalva

---

## Exercise Substitution Master List

Before the weekly breakdown, here are the key swaps already built into the programme. Share this with your client so she understands the reasoning.

| Traditional Exercise | Prenatal Substitute | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Flat bench press | Incline DB press (30–45°) or landmine press | No supine |
| Barbell back squat (heavy) | Goblet squat, safety bar squat, or box squat | IAP management, balance |
| Conventional deadlift (heavy) | Romanian deadlift, trap bar deadlift, or sumo | Belly clearance, IAP |
| Sit-ups / crunches | Dead bug (modified), pallof press | Diastasis risk |
| Prone exercises | Side-lying or standing alternatives | No prone after belly shows |
| Heavy overhead press | Seated DB press or landmine press | Reduces lumbar extension demand |
| Leg press (deep, heavy) | Moderate-depth leg press or step-ups | IAP and pelvic floor pressure |

---

## PHASE 1 — Weeks 1–4: Adaptation & Audit

**Phase goal:** Establish baseline, audit movement quality under the new constraints, introduce pelvic floor awareness into every session, and build the habit of modified training. Loads are deliberately conservative in Week 1 and build across the phase.

**Pelvic floor cue used every session:** Before each set, client performs a gentle pelvic floor contraction ("lift and hold"), releases it, then begins the movement. This is not Kegel overload — it is awareness-building.

---

### Week 1

**Session A — Lower Body Focus**

Begin each session with 8–10 minutes of warm-up: stationary bike or incline treadmill walk, hip circles, banded clamshells, cat-cow (on hands and knees), and thoracic rotations in a seated or side-lying position.

*Working sets:*

**1. Goblet Squat** — 4 sets × 10 reps. Hold a single dumbbell or kettlebell at chest height. Feet slightly wider than hip-width, toes turned out to accommodate the belly. Focus on controlled descent, upright torso, and exhale on the way up. Load: moderate — she should feel this is work but never a grind. Suggested starting point: 16–20 kg KB depending on her history.

**2. Romanian Deadlift (Barbell or DB)** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Hip hinge pattern, soft knee, bar or dumbbells tracking close to the legs. Stop the descent when she feels a strong hamstring stretch or when lower back begins to round — this point will rise as the belly grows. Load: 50–60% estimated 1RM.

**3. Hip Thrust (elevated on bench, feet flat)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Note: this is *not* supine — the upper back is on the bench, hips drive upward. This is safe and highly recommended for glute maintenance. Use a barbell across the hips with a pad, or a single heavy dumbbell held at the hip crease. Squeeze glutes at the top; do not hyperextend the lumbar spine.

**4. Single-Leg Press (moderate depth)** — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg. Foot positioned mid-platform. Do not allow the lower back to peel off the seat. Depth: to approximately 90 degrees — avoid deep compression that increases pelvic floor pressure.

**5. Standing Calf Raise** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Bodyweight or light load. Ankle swelling is common in pregnancy; this promotes circulation.

*Cool-down:* 5–8 minutes. Seated or side-lying hip flexor stretch, pigeon pose modified (seated figure-four), thoracic extension over a foam roller (upper back only, not lumbar), and diaphragmatic breathing — 5 slow breaths, expanding the ribcage 360 degrees.

---

**Session B — Upper Body Focus**

*Warm-up:* Band pull-aparts × 20, wall slides × 10, shoulder circles, light face pulls.

**1. Incline Dumbbell Press** — 4 sets × 10 reps. Bench set to 30–45 degrees. This replaces flat bench entirely. Dumbbells allow a more natural wrist and elbow path. Load: challenging but smooth — no arching, no breath-holding.

**2. Seated Cable Row or DB Bent-Over Row** — 4 sets × 10 reps. For the bent-over row, use a single-arm version with the opposite hand and knee supported on a bench. Maintain a neutral spine. Pull the elbow back and squeeze the scapula. Upper back strength is critical for postural support as the belly grows.

**3. Landmine Press** — 3 sets × 10 reps each side. One of the best pressing options in pregnancy. The angled bar path is shoulder-friendly, requires no supine position, and the standing or half-kneeling position engages the core appropriately. Half-kneeling is preferred — it also challenges hip flexor length.

**4. Lat Pulldown (wide or neutral grip)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Seated, upright posture. Avoid excessive lean-back. Pull to the upper chest, not behind the neck.

**5. Pallof Press** — 3 sets × 10 reps each side. Anti-rotation core work. Stand side-on to a cable stack or anchored band. Press the handle straight out from the chest and hold for 2 seconds, then return. This is one of the safest and most effective core exercises during pregnancy — it trains the deep stabilisers without spinal flexion or high IAP.

**6. Face Pull** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Rope attachment at eye level. External rotation and rear delt work. Excellent for counteracting the forward shoulder posture that pregnancy encourages.

*Cool-down:* Doorway chest stretch, lat stretch (standing, arm overhead gripping a rack), neck rolls, diaphragmatic breathing.

---

**Session C — Movement & Accessory (Lower Intensity)**

This session is not a rest day but a deliberate lower-intensity day. Heart rate should stay conversational. Think of it as "active maintenance."

**1. Incline Treadmill Walk** — 15 minutes at a comfortable pace. Incline 4–6%. This maintains cardiovascular conditioning without impact stress.

**2. Banded Glute Work Circuit** — 3 rounds:
- Banded clamshell × 15 each side
- Banded lateral walk × 10 steps each direction
- Banded glute bridge (supine is now contraindicated — use a *standing* banded hip abduction instead if she prefers, or the hip thrust position described above) × 15

**3. Step-Ups** — 3 sets × 12 reps each leg. Use a box at knee height or slightly below. Hold light dumbbells. Drive through the heel of the working leg. This is a fantastic unilateral lower body exercise that remains safe throughout pregnancy.

**4. Seated DB Shoulder Press** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Light to moderate load. Seated position reduces lumbar extension demand.

**5. Pelvic Floor & Breathing Work** — 10 minutes. This is non-negotiable and should be coached, not just assigned. Include: diaphragmatic breathing (5 reps, 5-second inhale, 5-second exhale), pelvic floor contractions (gentle lift and hold for 5 seconds, full release — emphasise the *release* as much as the contraction), and cat-cow on hands and knees.

---

### Weeks 2–4 — Progressive Overload Within Phase 1

Apply the following progression across Weeks 2, 3, and 4. Do not increase load and volume simultaneously.

**Week 2:** Add 1 working set to the primary compound movements in Sessions A and B (goblet squat goes to 5 sets, incline press goes to 5 sets). Load stays the same as Week 1 or increases by the smallest available increment if RPE felt below 6.

**Week 3:** Return to 4 working sets on compounds but increase load by 2.5–5 kg where RPE allows. Introduce a tempo element — 3-second eccentric on squats and RDLs to increase time under tension without adding load.

**Week 4:** Deload week. Reduce volume by 30–40% (drop to 3 sets on all exercises). Maintain load. Use this week to assess how she is feeling, check in on sleep quality, energy levels, and any new symptoms. This is also a good week to reassess movement quality — belly size will have changed meaningfully since Week 1.

---

## PHASE 2 — Weeks 5–8: Strength Maintenance

**Phase goal:** This is the heart of the programme. She is now 24–28 weeks pregnant. The belly is significant, centre of gravity has shifted, and relaxin levels are elevated (increasing joint laxity — be cautious with end-range loading). The goal is to maintain as much strength as possible while managing fatigue, which will be more variable than pre-pregnancy.

**Key Phase 2 adjustments:**
- Barbell back squat is retired if it feels uncomfortable or if bar position on the upper back becomes awkward. Safety bar squat or goblet squat continues.
- Conventional deadlift transitions fully to sumo or trap bar if not already done — belly clearance and a more upright torso are the priority.
- All overhead work is now seated to reduce lumbar extension demand.
- Monitor for symphysis pubis dysfunction (SPD) — if she reports groin or pelvic pain, eliminate single-leg work and wide-stance movements immediately and refer back to the OB.

---

### Week 5

**Session A — Lower Body**

**1. Safety Bar Squat or Goblet Squat** — 4 sets × 8 reps. Slightly heavier than Phase 1 peak loads. The safety bar is excellent here because it keeps the torso more upright and removes the need to reach back for a barbell. If the gym has one, prioritise it.

**2. Sumo Deadlift or Trap Bar Deadlift** — 4 sets × 6 reps. The sumo stance accommodates the belly naturally. The trap bar (if available) is arguably the best deadlift variation in pregnancy — more upright torso, handles at the sides rather than in front, and reduced shear on the lumbar spine. Load: 70–75% estimated 1RM. Exhale on the pull; no prolonged breath-holding.

**3. Hip Thrust** — 4 sets × 10 reps. Continue from Phase 1. This remains one of the most productive exercises she can do. Increase load if Phase 1 felt easy.

**4. Walking Lunge** — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg. Bodyweight or light dumbbells. Monitor balance carefully — offer a TRX or rack to hold if needed. If balance is a concern, substitute reverse lunges (more stable) or step-ups.

**5. Nordic Hamstring Curl (assisted) or Lying Leg Curl** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Hamstring integrity is important for pelvic stability. The lying leg curl machine is fine — she is face-down on the pad, which is acceptable as long as it is comfortable. If prone position is uncomfortable, substitute a standing cable leg curl.

**6. Standing Calf Raise** — 3 sets × 15 reps.

---

**Session B — Upper Body**

**1. Incline DB Press** — 4 sets × 8 reps. Increase load from Phase 1 if RPE allows.

**2. Barbell or DB Bent-Over Row** — 4 sets × 8 reps. If the belly makes the bilateral bent-over row uncomfortable, move fully to single-arm supported rows.

**3. Seated DB Overhead Press** — 4 sets × 8 reps. Seated, back supported or unsupported depending on comfort. Do not allow excessive lumbar arch.

**4. Neutral-Grip Lat Pulldown** — 3 sets × 10 reps.

**5. Cable Chest Fly (standing or seated)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. A good way to maintain chest work without any supine position. Set cables at shoulder height, stand in a split stance for stability.

**6. Pallof Press** — 3 sets × 12 reps each side. Increase resistance slightly from Phase 1.

**7. Rear Delt Fly (seated or standing)** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Light dumbbells. Postural work.

---

**Session C — Movement & Accessory**

**1. Stationary Bike or Swimming** — 20 minutes, easy effort. Swimming is particularly excellent in the second trimester — the water supports the belly and reduces joint stress. If she has access to a pool, encourage it strongly.

**2. Step-Ups** — 3 sets × 12 reps each leg. Increase box height slightly or add light dumbbells.

**3. TRX Row or Ring Row** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Body at an angle, pulling chest to handles. Excellent horizontal pull with no spinal loading.

**4. Banded Glute Circuit** — Same as Phase 1 but with slightly heavier bands.

**5. Pelvic Floor & Breathing** — 10 minutes. Continue every session.

---

### Weeks 6–8 — Progression Within Phase 2

**Week 6:** Increase load on primary lifts by 2.5–5 kg where RPE is 6 or below. Add a pause variation to one exercise per session — e.g., pause goblet squat (2-second pause at the bottom) or pause at the top of the hip thrust. Pauses increase difficulty without adding load, which is ideal for managing IAP.

**Week 7:** Volume peak for the programme. Add one additional working set to the two primary compound movements per session (squat/deadlift in Session A; press/row in Session B). This is the highest volume week of the entire 12 weeks. Monitor fatigue carefully — if she reports poor sleep, increased Braxton Hicks, or unusual swelling, pull back immediately.

**Week 8:** Deload. Same protocol as Week 4 — reduce volume by 30–40%, maintain load, prioritise movement quality and recovery. Use this week for a thorough check-in. She is now approximately 28 weeks pregnant. Ask about: pelvic girdle pain, round ligament pain, heartburn affecting training positions, and energy levels. Adjust Phase 3 accordingly.

---

## PHASE 3 — Weeks 9–12: Functional Strength & Longevity

**Phase goal:** She is now 28–32 weeks pregnant. The third trimester brings increased fatigue, more significant postural changes, and greater pelvic floor demand. The goal shifts from strength maintenance to *functional strength preservation* — keeping the movements she will need for labour, recovery, and early motherhood. Volume decreases, intensity (relative effort) stays moderate, and movement quality is the primary metric.

**Key Phase 3 adjustments:**
- RPE cap drops to 6–7. No set should feel like a true struggle.
- Reduce bilateral barbell work further. Unilateral and machine-based work becomes more prominent — it is easier to manage load and position.
- Introduce more wall-supported and seated variations as needed.
- Increase rest periods to 2–3 minutes between sets without apology.
- Session duration may naturally shorten to 45–50 minutes as she fatigues more quickly.
- Continue monitoring for any new symptoms: increased pelvic pressure, leaking with exertion (a sign of pelvic floor overload — reduce load immediately and refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist), or significant diastasis symptoms (coning or doming at the midline during exertion).

---

### Week 9

**Session A — Lower Body**

**1. Goblet Squat or Safety Bar Squat** — 3 sets × 8 reps. Load maintained from Phase 2 peak or slightly reduced based on comfort. Quality over quantity.

**2. Trap Bar Deadlift or Sumo Deadlift** — 3 sets × 6 reps. Same load as Phase 2 or a small reduction. Focus on bracing, breathing, and a clean hinge pattern.

**3. Hip Thrust** — 3 sets × 10 reps. This exercise remains productive and comfortable well into the third trimester for most women.

**4. Reverse Lunge (holding rack or TRX for balance)** — 3 sets × 8 reps each leg. Balance support is now offered as standard, not optional.

**5. Seated Leg Curl** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Seated variation preferred over prone in the third trimester.

**6. Standing Calf Raise** — 2 sets × 15 reps.

---

**Session B — Upper Body**

**1. Incline DB Press** — 3 sets × 8 reps.

**2. Single-Arm DB Row** — 3 sets × 10 reps each side. Supported on a bench. This remains one of the most comfortable rowing variations as the belly grows.

**3. Seated DB Overhead Press** — 3 sets × 8 reps.

**4. Neutral-Grip Lat Pulldown** — 3 sets × 10 reps.

**5. Standing Cable Chest Fly** — 3 sets × 12 reps.

**6. Face Pull** — 3 sets × 15 reps.

**7. Pallof Press** — 3 sets × 10 reps each side.

---

**Session C — Movement & Accessory**

**1. Swimming or Stationary Bike** — 20–25 minutes, easy effort. Swimming is strongly encouraged in the third trimester.

**2. Step-Ups** — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg. Bodyweight or very light load.

**3. TRX Row** — 3 sets × 12 reps.

**4. Banded Glute Work** — 2 rounds of the circuit from Phase 2.

**5. Pelvic Floor & Breathing** — 10–15 minutes. Increase time on this component in Phase 3. Include: diaphragmatic breathing, pelvic floor contractions and releases, and child's pose (modified — knees wide to accommodate belly) for relaxation.

---

### Weeks 10–12 — Managing the Final Stretch

**Week 10:** Maintain Week 9 loads. Do not attempt to progress load in Phase 3 unless she explicitly feels under-challenged and RPE is consistently below 5. The priority is consistency and safety, not progression.

**Week 11:** Reduce volume by one set on all compound movements (3 sets becomes 2 sets). Maintain load. She is now approximately 31 weeks pregnant. Fatigue, sleep disruption, and physical discomfort are likely to be more significant. Honour that. A shorter, well-executed session is far more valuable than a full session done poorly or abandoned.

**Week 12:** Programme conclusion. This week is intentionally light — think of it as a celebration of 12 weeks of consistent, intelligent training. Perform two sessions only (drop Session A or B, keep Session C). Use loads that feel comfortable and movements that feel good. End each session with an extended cool-down and breathing practice. Discuss the plan for Weeks 32 onward with the OB — many women continue modified training to 36–38 weeks with appropriate adjustments.

---

## Nutrition Guidelines

*Note to trainer: These are general evidence-based principles. Refer to a registered dietitian for individualised guidance, particularly given the pregnancy.*

**Caloric needs:** Pregnancy requires approximately 300–350 additional calories per day in the second trimester, rising to 450–500 in the third. With moderate strength training, she should not be in a caloric deficit at any point. Undereating during pregnancy is a significant risk — prioritise adequate intake above all else.

**Protein:** Aim for 1.6–1.8 g per kg of bodyweight per day. Protein supports both her muscle maintenance and foetal development. Distribute across 4–5 meals or eating occasions. Good sources: eggs, Greek yoghurt, lean meats, fish (low-mercury options: salmon, sardines, trout), legumes, and dairy.

**Carbohydrates:** Do not restrict. Carbohydrates fuel training and support foetal brain development. Prioritise complex sources: oats, sweet potato, rice, fruit, and whole grains. A small carbohydrate-containing snack 30–60 minutes before training helps maintain energy and prevents dizziness.

**Fats:** Omega-3 fatty acids (DHA in particular) are critical for foetal neurological development. Encourage fatty fish 2–3 times per week or a high-quality algae-based DHA supplement (preferred over fish oil for purity in pregnancy).

**Hydration:** Dehydration can trigger Braxton Hicks contractions and increases fatigue. Target a minimum of 2.5–3 litres of water per day, more on training days. She should arrive at every session already well-hydrated.

**Iron:** Pregnancy increases iron demand significantly. If she is not already supplementing (most prenatal vitamins include iron), encourage her to discuss iron levels with her OB. Low iron will tank her training energy.

**Pre-training:** Light meal or snack 60–90 minutes before training. Example: Greek yoghurt with banana and a handful of granola, or two eggs on toast with avocado.

**Post-training:** Protein and carbohydrate within 60 minutes. Example: protein shake with milk and a piece of fruit, or chicken and rice.

---

## Recovery Guidelines

**Sleep:** The single most important recovery tool. Encourage side-sleeping (left side preferred for circulation) with a pregnancy pillow supporting the belly and between the knees. If she is waking frequently, discuss with her OB — this is normal but worth monitoring.

**Rest days:** There should be at least one full rest day between each training session. With three sessions per week, a Monday/Wednesday/Friday or Tuesday/Thursday/Saturday split works well. Avoid training on consecutive days.

**Active recovery:** On non-training days, gentle walking (20–30 minutes) is encouraged and beneficial. It maintains cardiovascular conditioning, reduces swelling
